subject: Cooking
title: From Ethiopia to the World: Coffee's Global Journey
description: A micro-lesson that makes From Ethiopia to the World: Coffee's Global Journey usable.

hook.text: Yemen tried to control the coffee trade by boiling beans before export — making them infertile. It didn't work.

buildup.text: Sufi monks in Yemen were the first systematic coffee brewers — creating the port of Mocha as the trade hub.

discovery.text: Dutch traders smuggled live coffee plants to Java (Indonesia) in 1616 — breaking Yemen's monopoly.

twist.text: A single coffee plant gifted to France's King Louis XIV in 1714 became the ancestor of all Caribbean coffee.

climax.text: Brazil — now the world's largest producer — got its first coffee plants through a diplomat's secret love affair.

punchline.text: Smuggling, theft, and romance spread coffee across the globe.

quiz.question: How did the Dutch break Yemen's coffee monopoly?
options: Smuggling live coffee plants to Java

details.summary: Coffee traveled from Ethiopian forests to Yemeni monasteries, then to Ottoman coffee houses, European cafés, and colonial plantations across the tropics. The Dutch smuggled coffee plants to Java in the 1600s. The French brought a single plant to the Caribbean.
details.whyItMatters: Coffee's global journey maps colonial expansion, smuggling, and botanical espionage. A plant from Ethiopian forests became the second most traded commodity after oil through centuries of theft and cultivation.
takeaways: Coffee moved from Ethiopia to Yemen to the Ottoman Empire to Europe
Colonial powers smuggled plants to establish tropical plantations
Brazil's massive industry traces to seeds smuggled in 1727

faq.question: How did coffee spread from Ethiopia to the rest of the world?
faq.answer: Ethiopian coffee crossed the Red Sea to Yemen where Sufi monks cultivated it. Ottoman traders brought it to Istanbul. Venetian merchants introduced it to Europe.

faq.question: Why was coffee called the devil's drink in Europe?
faq.answer: Catholic priests initially viewed coffee suspiciously because it came from Muslim lands and stimulated the mind. Some called it Satan's drink. Pope Clement VIII allegedly tasted it, declared it delicious, and baptized it to make it acceptable for Christians, ending the religious objections.
